title: RISC-V playground
intro: Write and run your own code in the course workbench. Open Tools for inspection, setup and projects.

links.homeDescription: Use the course workbench for your own projects. Each project keeps its source and starting setup together.
guideParagraphs: Use the lesson’s example and optional exercise for guided work. To keep an independent experiment, open Tools → Projects and choose Save a copy. The project opens in the same editor with its own source and starting setup.
A copy of an exercise uses the selected case’s inputs and data. Project edits keep the lesson draft unchanged. Choose Return to lesson to restore the example or exercise you left.
Open the playground from the course overview to work on independent projects. In a lesson, use Tools → Projects to keep working in the same editor.

projectTypes.label: Assembly fragment
projectTypes.description: Write the instructions you want to investigate. Supplied code starts the program, captures registers and exits.
projectTypes.sourceHelp: Write assembly instructions. View complete program shows the supplied entry, reporting and exit code.
projectTypes.entryHelp: The lab supplies entry, register capture and exit code around your assembly fragment.
projectTypes.completeSourceDescription: This is your fragment inside the supplied entry, capture and exit code. The supplied code prepares the listed inputs and records registers and memory before printing the report.

projectTypes.label: C function
projectTypes.description: Write a function named lesson. The supplied caller passes its arguments and captures its result.
projectTypes.sourceHelp: Define lesson with two long arguments. Starting registers a0 and a1 supply the arguments; a0 receives the returned value.
projectTypes.entryHelp: The lab supplies a caller that passes the starting arguments to lesson, captures registers and exits.
projectTypes.completeSourceDescription: This view contains your C function and its supplied assembly caller. The caller prepares the listed arguments, captures registers and memory, prints the report and exits.

projectTypes.label: Complete assembly program
projectTypes.description: Define _start, the program’s entry label. Your source controls initialisation, data and exit.
projectTypes.sourceHelp: Define _start and include your program’s exit code. Start stepping or Start debugging to inspect registers while it runs.
projectTypes.entryHelp: Your program defines _start and supplies its own initialisation, data and exit code. No entry or reporting code is added.
projectTypes.completeSourceDescription: This is your complete assembly source, used unchanged for the build. Its entry, initialisation, data and exit belong to the program. No final register report is added.

setup.intro: Set the values supplied before your code starts. Apply setup ends the current run; the next build starts a fresh machine.
setup.registerHelp: Use one assignment per line, such as t0 = 7. Decimal is the default; use 0x for hexadecimal or 0b for binary. Values must fit 64 bits.
setup.reservedHelp: The starting setup does not accept zero, sp, gp or tp. The supplied code prepares the stack pointer; zero always reads zero.
setup.dataHelp: Use pairs of hexadecimal digits separated by spaces, such as 01 FF. Up to 64 bytes; remaining bytes start at zero.
setup.memoryHelp: Data shows 64 bytes from lesson_data. Stack shows 64 bytes from the observed stack pointer, sp.
setup.highlightHelp: Marks a register in the inspector. It does not change execution.
setup.fullProgramHelp: A complete assembly program supplies its own initialisation and data. Set those values in the source.
setup.fullProgramMemoryHelp: The Data view starts at lesson_data if your program defines that symbol. Otherwise it starts at the first loaded writable region, or the first code region if none is writable. Stack starts at the observed sp.
setup.lessonHelp: Apply setup opens a project copy with these values. Your lesson draft and its starting setup stay unchanged.

help.title: Source and execution
paragraphs: The editor and run controls work the same way in lessons and independent projects. Open Tools when you need more inspection, starting setup or saved projects. Close Tools to concentrate on the code and its relevant results.
Program shows your current source inside its complete program. Expand a supplied section to inspect the setup, capture or reporting code. Your fragment stays editable in the editor.
Machine instructions shows the executable from your last successful build. Build again after editing the source. During stepping, PC marks the next instruction to execute.
Registers shows observations from execution. Pin useful registers, compare changed values, or choose All to see every integer register.

help.title: Choose the source you want to write
paragraphs: An assembly fragment is a group of instructions inside a supplied program. You can concentrate on those instructions; View complete program shows the entry, reporting and exit code around them.

A C project defines a function named lesson, such as long lesson(long a, long b). The supplied caller passes a0 and a1 as its arguments and captures the return value in a0. Do not add main, system headers or library calls.
A complete assembly program defines _start and includes its own exit code. Its registers and data come from its source and xv6, so the fragment’s starting-register and data controls do not apply.

help.title: Run and inspect
paragraphs: Build & Run assembles and links your source, then runs it as an xv6 user process. C projects first compile their function with TinyCC. Every new run starts a fresh machine.
Start stepping pauses before your first machine instruction. Step instruction executes one machine instruction. A source line can expand into several machine instructions.

A breakpoint pauses before its instruction runs. Choose the numbered button beside an assembly instruction, then use Start debugging. Continue runs to a selected breakpoint or the end of your code. For C, select actual instruction addresses in Debugger; this compiler does not provide C source-line mappings.

Register and memory readings belong to the observation named beside them. Assembly fragments and C functions capture a report after their code. Complete programs can exit without that report: a last paused observation is not an exit state.

help.title: Supply starting values
paragraphs: For fragments and C functions, Setup supplies register values before your source runs. Use assignments such as t0 = 7, one per line. Apply setup commits the entries and ends the current run. Editing the setup form alone does not change a paused machine.
Data bytes fills the area named lesson_data. Hexadecimal uses digits 0–9 and A–F; two hexadecimal digits describe one byte. Unspecified bytes start at zero.
Memory view chooses the 64-byte region shown in Memory. Data starts at lesson_data. Stack starts at the observed stack pointer, sp. The Stack tab and memory watches provide further observed readings.

help.title: Keep your projects
paragraphs: Source and setup save together in this browser when storage is available. Check the save message. A project saves your code and setup, not a running or paused machine.

Open Tools → Projects to open a saved project, choose an example, import a file or create a new project. Open example and Import file create new projects and keep your other work. Save a copy keeps the current source and setup in another project.
From a lesson, Save a copy opens an independent project in the same editor. The lesson draft stays available through Return to lesson. An exercise copy uses the selected case’s inputs and data.

Export project saves the source and setup in one JSON file. Download code saves only the source. Import file accepts project JSON, assembly source (.s or .asm), or C source (.c). Check Import as before opening a source file.
If storage is unavailable, you can keep working in this tab. Export project before leaving to keep that work. Delete project can be reversed with Undo delete.

help.title: Know the execution environment
paragraphs: Programs target 64-bit RISC-V and run in xv6. Its system calls differ from Linux and teaching simulators. In this guest, write is system call 16 and exit is system call 2.
The playground supplies console output, but no console input. The guest does not provide floating-point process state. Stepping shows functional execution, not physical hardware timing.

workspace.fragmentIntro: Your code sits inside the supplied program. Expand the folded sections to inspect its setup and reporting code.
workspace.programIntro: This is your complete source. The build uses it unchanged.
workspace.cIntro: Your C function and its supplied assembly caller are separate source files. Build the program to inspect the compiled instructions.
workspace.noBuild: Build or start stepping to see the instructions in the executable.
workspace.buildNote: Last successful build. PC marks the next instruction at the last pause. One assembly source line can produce several instructions.
workspace.stale: Source changed. Instructions and observations still belong to the previous build. Build again to use your edits.
workspace.cMapping: TinyCC does not provide C source-line mappings. This scope shows the compiled lesson function.
workspace.allScope: All includes supplied setup, helper functions and reporting code.
workspace.filterHelp: Pinned keeps chosen registers together. Changed compares values with the preceding observation. All shows every integer register.
workspace.emptyRegisters: No registers match this view. Pin a register from All, or run or step to compare values.
workspace.noInstructions: This build emitted no instructions in this scope.
workspace.cAllMapping: TinyCC does not provide C source-line mappings. All includes compiled C and the supplied assembly.
